issues.legal_issue: A dispute over the non-employment of staff by an incoming management is an industrial dispute when the workmen as a class have a direct or substantial interest in that employment.
material_facts: The outgoing management gave the staff notice terminating their services while conciliation proceedings were pending.
The dispute concerned whether the incoming management could refuse to continue the staff’s employment and service conditions.
The staff whose employment was in dispute were persons in whose employment or non-employment the estate’s workmen were directly interested.
issues.conclusion: The reference was a competent reference of an industrial dispute under the Industrial Disputes Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, a dispute raised by workmen can concern the employment or non-employment of persons who are not themselves strictly workmen, provided the workmen as a class have a direct or substantial interest in that employment or non-employment. The Court applied Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate and Western India Automobile Association v. Industrial Tribunal, Bombay.

predicates.industrial_dispute_reference: A government referred a dispute between workmen and management concerning employment or non-employment for industrial adjudication.
predicates.workmen_directly_interested: The workmen as a class had a direct or substantial interest in the employment or non-employment of the persons concerned.
predicates.employment_or_nonemployment_is_disputed: The parties disputed whether the persons concerned would be employed or retained in employment.

issues.definition: When a dispute referred for industrial adjudication concerns employment or non-employment in which the workmen as a class have a direct or substantial interest, the reference is competent.

issues.legal_issue: An industrial tribunal may decide a referred employment dispute and make an order based on the proven circumstances of the dispute, and an appellate tribunal errs by treating the dispute as an abstract question of contractual liability while leaving the material findings undisturbed.
material_facts: The estate was transferred as a going concern, and all manual labourers continued on their previous terms with continuity of service.

Three staff members were retained as new recruits without continuity of service, while the remaining staff were not taken on despite the tribunal finding no trade or efficiency reason for that decision.

The incoming management required staff members to apply afresh and accept new employment without continuity of service, conditions the tribunal found discriminatory and likely to cause industrial unrest.
The outgoing management gave notice of termination during pending conciliation proceedings, and the staff continued working until 4 January 1954.

The industrial tribunal ordered reinstatement on the previous terms with continuity of service and payment of salary for forced unemployment; the appellate tribunal set aside the award without displacing the industrial tribunal’s material findings.
issues.conclusion: The industrial tribunal had jurisdiction to make its order on its findings, irrespective of whether a contractual employment relationship existed between the incoming management and the discharged staff. The Court set aside the appellate tribunal’s decision and restored the industrial tribunal’s award.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(1)(c) and 10(4) of the Industrial Disputes Act, a tribunal adjudicates the dispute referred to it and confines its adjudication to the specified points and matters incidental to them. Its function is to decide the dispute on its facts, not to answer abstract questions of law detached from the parties’ contractual rights and the circumstances. The Court relied on Niemla Textile Finishing Mills, Ltd. v. Second Punjab Industrial Tribunal in describing the functions of industrial tribunals. It also held that the outgoing management’s termination notice, given while conciliation proceedings were pending, was hit by Section 33 of the Act.

rule.if: appeal_against_reversal_of_industrial_award and competent_industrial_reference and (transfer_as_going_concern and existing_workers_continued and no_business_reason_for_excluding_staff) and incoming_management_imposed_discriminatory_fresh_terms and termination_notice_during_conciliation and material_findings_not_displaced

predicates.appeal_against_reversal_of_industrial_aw: An appeal challenged an appellate decision that had set aside an industrial tribunal’s award.
predicates.competent_industrial_reference: The government referred a dispute that qualified as an industrial dispute for adjudication.
predicates.transfer_as_going_concern: The business was transferred as a continuing operation rather than closed down.
predicates.existing_workers_continued: The manual labourers continued working on their previous terms with continuity of service after the transfer.
predicates.no_business_reason_for_excluding_staff: The industrial tribunal found no trade, efficiency, or similar business reason for excluding the staff members who were not retained.
predicates.incoming_management_imposed_discriminato: The incoming management required staff members to seek fresh appointments without continuity of service while other workers continued on their previous terms.
predicates.termination_notice_during_conciliation: The outgoing management gave the staff notice of termination while conciliation proceedings were pending.
predicates.material_findings_not_displaced: The appellate tribunal did not displace the industrial tribunal’s material findings about the transfer, continued employment, and exclusion of staff.

issues.definition: When an appeal reverses an industrial award despite an undisplaced factual basis showing a continuing operation, continued employment of other workers, discriminatory exclusion of staff without business reasons, and termination during conciliation, the industrial award is restored.
